sk: अथ हैनं सुकेशा भारद्वाजः पप्रच्छ भगवन्हिरण्यनाभः कौसल्यो राजपुत्रो मामुपेत्यैतं प्रश्नमपृच्छत षोडशकलं भारद्वाज पुरुषं वेत्थ तमहं कुमारमब्रुवं नाहमिमं वेद यद्यहमिममवेदिषमकथं ते नावक्ष्यमसमूलो ह्येष परिशुष्यति यो ऽनृतमभिवदति तस्मान्नार्हाम्यनृतं वक्तुम् स तूष्णीं रथमारुह्य प्रवव्राज तं त्वा पृच्छामि क्वासौ पुरुष इति ||
ro: atha · ha · enaṁ · sukeśāḥ · bhāradvājaḥ · papraccha · bhagavan · hiraṇyanābhaḥ · kausalyaḥ · rāja-putraḥ · mām · upetya · etaṁ · praśnam · apṛcchata · ṣoḍaśa-kalaṁ · bhāradvāja · puruṣaṁ · vettha · tam · ahaṁ · kumāram · abruvam · na · aham · imaṁ · veda · yadi · aham · imam · avediṣam · kathaṁ · te · na · avakṣyam · asamūlaḥ · hi · eṣaḥ · pariśuṣyati · yaḥ · anṛtam · abhivadati · tasmāt · na · arhāmi · anṛtaṁ · vaktum · saḥ · tūṣṇīṁ · ratham · āruhya · pravavrāja · taṁ · tvā · pṛcchāmi · kva · asau · puruṣaḥ · iti ||
hi: तब सुकेशा भारद्वाज ने (पिप्पलाद से) पूछा — 'भगवन्! हिरण्यनाभ कौसल्य नामक राजपुत्र ने मेरे पास आकर यह प्रश्न पूछा: "हे भारद्वाज! क्या तुम षोडशकल (सोलह कलाओं वाले) पुरुष को जानते हो?" तब मैंने उस कुमार (राजकुमार) से कहा — "मैं इसे नहीं जानता। यदि मैं इसे जानता, तो तुम्हें क्यों न बताता? निश्चय ही जो असत्य (अनृत) बोलता है, वह जड़-सहित (समूल) सूख जाता है। इसलिए मैं असत्य बोलने योग्य नहीं हूँ।" वह (राजकुमार) मौन होकर (तूष्णीम्) रथ पर चढ़कर चला गया। उन्हीं (षोडशकल पुरुष) के विषय में मैं आपसे पूछता हूँ — वह पुरुष कहाँ (क्व) है?'
en: Then Sukeśā Bhāradvāja asked him: 'Bhagavan! Hiraṇyanābha Kausalya, a prince, came to me and asked this question: "O Bhāradvāja! Do you know the Person (Puruṣa) with sixteen parts (ṣoḍaśa-kala)?" I said to that young man: "I do not know him. If I knew, why would I not tell you? Surely, he who speaks untruth dries up root and all (asamūlaḥ pariśuṣyati). Therefore I am not fit to speak untruth." He silently (tūṣṇīm) mounted his chariot and departed. About that (Puruṣa) I ask you — where is that Person?'

ws.h: जड़-सहित सूख जाता है / समूल नष्ट हो जाता है

gr: A story within a story: Sukeśā's question is unique among the six — it comes with a narrative backstory. A prince (Hiraṇyanābha Kausalya) had already asked Sukeśā about the sixteen-part Puruṣa, and Sukeśā honestly admitted ignorance. This story serves multiple purposes: (1) It demonstrates intellectual honesty (satya-niṣṭhā) — Sukeśā refused to pretend knowledge he didn't have. (2) The curse-formula (asamūlaḥ pariśuṣyati) shows the Vedic terror of untruth — a liar 'dries up root and all'. (3) It establishes the question's difficulty — even a learned brāhmaṇa like Sukeśā couldn't answer it. ṣoḍaśa-kala puruṣa: the Person with sixteen parts. This is not a physical anatomy but a metaphysical structure — the sixteen kalās (parts/phases) from which the manifest world is constituted and into which it resolves. kva asau puruṣaḥ — 'where is that Person?': not 'where is he located?' but 'what/where is the Puruṣa in whom the sixteen kalās subsist?' The question asks for the ground of the sixteen parts.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — सुकेशा की ईमानदारी (honesty) आदर्श शिष्य का लक्षण है — 'नाहमिमं वेद' — 'मैं नहीं जानता' कहने का साहस। अज्ञान स्वीकार करना ज्ञान का प्रथम चरण है। 'षोडशकल पुरुष' = सगुण ब्रह्म — जिसकी सोलह कलाएँ सृष्टि की सोलह तत्त्व-धाराएँ हैं।
advaita.en: Shankara says Sukeśā's honesty is the mark of an ideal disciple — 'nāham imam veda' — the courage to say 'I do not know.' Admitting ignorance is the first step to knowledge. 'Ṣoḍaśa-kala puruṣa' = saguṇa Brahman — whose sixteen kalās are the sixteen streams of manifestation.
advaita.ins: The bravest thing Sukeśā said was: 'I don't know.' A scholar who admits ignorance is more honest than one who fabricates knowledge. That admission is what brought him to Pippalāda — and what brings us to the deepest teaching.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'अनृतमभिवदति असमूलः परिशुष्यति' — सत्य (truth) का उल्लंघन विनाशकारी है। सुकेशा ने भगवान् के प्रति सत्यनिष्ठा (truth-commitment) से अपनी अज्ञानता स्वीकार की — यह भक्ति का लक्षण है। 'षोडशकल पुरुष' = भगवान् नारायण — जिनकी सोलह कलाएँ सृष्टि के सोलह तत्त्व हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'anṛtam abhivadati asamūlaḥ pariśuṣyati' — violating truth is destructive. Sukeśā's truth-commitment in admitting ignorance is a mark of devotion. 'Ṣoḍaśa-kala puruṣa' = Lord Nārāyaṇa — whose sixteen kalās are the sixteen elements of creation.
vishisht.ins: A prince asked a question. The scholar could have faked an answer — no one would have known. But he said: 'I don't know. And I won't pretend I do, because liars are destroyed.' That integrity is more valuable than the answer itself.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — सुकेशा की कथा बौद्धिक ईमानदारी (intellectual honesty) का उदाहरण है — जो आध्यात्मिक विकास (spiritual growth) की पूर्वशर्त (prerequisite) है। 'षोडशकल पुरुष' = चेतन पुरुष (Conscious Being) — जिसकी सोलह कलाएँ चेतना की सोलह शक्तियाँ (powers) हैं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says Sukeśā's story exemplifies intellectual honesty — a prerequisite for spiritual growth. 'Ṣoḍaśa-kala puruṣa' = the Conscious Being — whose sixteen kalās are the sixteen powers of consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: Before you can learn anything real, you have to be able to say: 'I don't know.' Sukeśā could have performed knowledge. Instead, he performed honesty. And that's what qualified him to receive the answer from Pippalāda.

dp.a: Hiraṇyanābha Kausalya ('Golden-navelled, of the Kosala dynasty') was a prince (rāja-putra) who appears in several Vedic and post-Vedic texts: (1) In the Prashna Upanishad: he approaches Sukeśā Bhāradvāja with the question about the sixteen-part Puruṣa. When Sukeśā honestly admits ignorance, the prince silently departs — showing both his gravity (he doesn't argue) and his respect (he doesn't disparage Sukeśā). (2) In the Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra (16.1.1): Hiraṇyanābha is mentioned as a promulgator of the Sāma Veda tradition, suggesting he was both a political ruler and a spiritual teacher. (3) In the later tradition: Hiraṇyanābha is sometimes identified with a king of the Kosala dynasty (the dynasty that ruled Ayodhyā). Some commentators connect him to the Iṣvāku lineage (Rāma's dynasty). The significance of the story: a prince asking a brāhmaṇa a question the brāhmaṇa cannot answer illustrates that spiritual knowledge is not the monopoly of any class. It also shows the difficulty of the question — the ṣoḍaśa-kalā doctrine was evidently not widely known even among learned brāhmaṇas. The prince's silent departure (tūṣṇīṁ ratham āruhya pravavrāja) is a mark of kṣatriya dignity — he doesn't press, argue, or mock. He accepts the honest answer and moves on.

Sukeśā's refusal to speak untruth reflects the absolute centrality of truth (satya) in the Vedic ethical system: The curse-formula: 'asamūlaḥ pariśuṣyati yaḥ anṛtam abhivadati' — 'he who speaks untruth dries up root and all.' This is not a metaphor but a cosmic law in the Vedic worldview: untruth (anṛta) violates ṛta (cosmic order), and the violator is destroyed by that same order. The image of drying up 'root and all' (asamūla) suggests complete annihilation — not just punishment but existential collapse. Parallels: (1) The Chāndogya's ordeal-by-truth (6.16): a suspected thief holds a heated axe. If he speaks untruth, it burns him. Truth physically protects. (2) The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (1.4.14): 'Truth is Dharma... He who speaks truth speaks Dharma; he who speaks Dharma speaks truth. They are the same thing.' (3) The Taittirīya's convocation address (1.11): 'Satyaṁ vada' — 'Speak truth' — is the first commandment given to the graduating student. Sukeśā's application: for Sukeśā, the ethic of truth applies not only to moral situations but to intellectual ones. To claim knowledge one does not have is a form of untruth — and carries the same cosmic consequences. This principle makes him an ideal student: only one who admits ignorance can genuinely learn.

sk: तस्मै स होवाचैहैवान्तःशरीरे सोम्य स पुरुषो यस्मिन्नेताः षोडश कलाः प्रभवन्तीति ||
ro: tasmai · saḥ · ha · uvāca · iha · eva · antaḥ-śarīre · somya · saḥ · puruṣaḥ · yasmin · etāḥ · ṣoḍaśa · kalāḥ · prabhavanti · iti ||
hi: उनसे उन्होंने (पिप्पलाद ने) कहा — 'हे सोम्य (प्रिय शिष्य)! यहीं इसी शरीर के भीतर (इह एव अन्तःशरीरे) वह पुरुष है — जिसमें ये सोलह कलाएँ उत्पन्न होती हैं (प्रभवन्ति)।'
en: To him he said: 'Here, within this very body (iha eva antaḥ-śarīre), O dear one (somya), is that Person (Puruṣa) in whom these sixteen parts (kalāḥ) arise (prabhavanti).'

ws.h: हे सौम्य / हे प्रिय / हे सुशील
उत्पन्न होती हैं / प्रकट होती हैं

gr: iha eva antaḥ-śarīre — 'right here, within this body': Pippalāda's answer is startling in its immediacy. The prince had asked 'where is that Puruṣa?' as if it were far away. Pippalāda says: right here, in your own body. This is the characteristic Upanishadic move — redirecting the search from the external to the internal. somya: a tender address ('O gentle one') famously used by Uddālaka Āruṇi in the Chāndogya ('tat tvam asi, somya' — 'you are that, dear one'). Its use here signals an intimate, transformative teaching. yasmin etāḥ ṣoḍaśa kalāḥ prabhavanti — 'in whom these sixteen kalās arise': the Puruṣa is the source (prabhava) of the sixteen kalās. They come from him, subsist in him, and (as the next mantras will show) resolve back into him. The question 'where is the Puruṣa?' is answered: he is the source within you.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'इह एव अन्तःशरीरे' — पुरुष कहीं बाहर नहीं, इसी शरीर में है। सोलह कलाएँ उस पुरुष से उत्पन्न (prabhavanti) होती हैं — जैसे किरणें सूर्य से। पुरुष = निर्गुण ब्रह्म — कलाएँ = उसकी माया-शक्ति से प्रकट अभिव्यक्तियाँ।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'iha eva antaḥ-śarīre' — the Puruṣa is not somewhere outside but right here in the body. The sixteen kalās originate from that Puruṣa — as rays from the sun. Puruṣa = nirguṇa Brahman; kalās = manifestations projected by His māyā-śakti.
advaita.ins: You don't need to travel to find the Puruṣa. He is here — in you. The sixteen parts that make up your experience all come from Him. Finding the source means looking inward, not outward.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'इह अन्तःशरीरे' — भगवान् प्रत्येक जीव के शरीर में अन्तर्यामी (inner controller) रूप में विद्यमान हैं। सोलह कलाएँ भगवान् की शक्ति (power) से प्रकट होती हैं — भगवान् उनका आश्रय (substratum) हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'iha antaḥ-śarīre' — the Lord is present in every being's body as the antaryāmin (inner controller). The sixteen kalās manifest through the Lord's power — the Lord is their substratum.
vishisht.ins: The Person you're looking for isn't far away. He's in you — the inner controller of every living body. The sixteen parts of your experience are His powers. Find Him inside, and you find the source of everything.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'इह अन्तःशरीरे' — चेतन पुरुष (Conscious Being) शरीर में उपस्थित है — न कहीं दूर, न किसी अन्य लोक में। सोलह कलाएँ उसी चेतना की सोलह शक्ति-धाराएँ (power-streams) हैं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'iha antaḥ-śarīre' — the Conscious Being is present within the body — not distant, not in another world. The sixteen kalās are sixteen power-streams of that same consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: The Puruṣa is not in heaven. He's in you — right now, reading these words. The sixteen parts are His expressions, His powers. He is the ocean; the sixteen parts are His waves.

dp.a: The word kalā (कला) is rich with meanings, all relevant to this context: (1) Moon-digit: the moon passes through sixteen phases (ṣoḍaśa kalāḥ) — from new moon (amāvāsyā, zero visible digits) through full moon (pūrṇimā, sixteen visible digits) and back. Each night, one 'digit' is added or subtracted. The sixteenth kalā — the invisible one that persists even at new moon — is the metaphor for the Puruṣa: the imperishable remainder when all parts are subtracted. (2) Part/constituent: in philosophical usage, kalā means a constituent element of a composite reality. The sixteen kalās of the Puruṣa are the sixteen elements from which manifest existence is constituted (enumerated in the next mantra). (3) Art/skill: in later usage, kalā means 'art' or 'skill' (as in the sixty-four kalās of classical education). This meaning is secondary here but suggests that the Puruṣa's self-expression through sixteen parts is an 'art' — a creative act. The moon-metaphor is primary: the Chāndogya (6.7) uses the same image — a fire of sixteen flames, reduced one by one until only the wick remains. The wick = prāṇa (life). Similarly, the sixteen kalās of the Puruṣa can be 'subtracted' one by one (in deep sleep, in death), but the Puruṣa himself — the sixteenth-plus-one, the imperishable ground — remains.

dp.q: 🔍 'Right here, within this body' — the Upanishadic immanence principle
dp.a: Pippalāda's answer 'iha eva antaḥ-śarīre' ('right here, within this body') expresses the central Upanishadic principle of immanence: the ultimate reality is not distant but present within every living being. This principle appears throughout the principal Upanishads: Kaṭha 1.2.20: 'The Self, smaller than the small, greater than the great, is set in the heart (hṛdaya) of every creature.' Chāndogya 6.8.7: 'Tat tvam asi, Śvetaketu' — 'You are That, Śvetaketu.' The ultimate reality (tat) is identified with the individual self (tvam). Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.4.1: 'This is your Self (ātman) that is within all' (ya eṣa sarvabhūtāntarātmā). Muṇḍaka 2.1.10: 'The Puruṣa alone is all this.' Māṇḍūkya 2: 'This Self (ātman) is Brahman. This same Self has four quarters.' Why 'within the body'? The body (śarīra) is the laboratory of Upanishadic inquiry. You don't need to travel to a cosmic realm to find the Puruṣa — you need to look within. The five senses point outward (parāñci — Kaṭha 2.1.1), but the wise one turns the gaze inward (pratyagātman) and discovers the Puruṣa right where he always was — in the cave of the heart (guhā), in the centre of one's own being.

sk: स ईक्षत कस्मिन्नहमुत्क्रान्त उत्क्रान्तो भविष्यामि कस्मिन्वा प्रतिष्ठिते प्रतिष्ठास्यामीति ||
ro: saḥ · īkṣata · kasmin · aham · utkrāntaḥ · utkrāntaḥ · bhaviṣyāmi · kasmin · vā · pratiṣṭhite · pratiṣṭhāsyāmi · iti ||
hi: उसने (पुरुष ने) ईक्षण (विचार/संकल्प) किया — 'मैं किसमें उत्क्रान्त (departed / बाहर निकला) होकर (सब कुछ) उत्क्रान्त होगा? और किसमें प्रतिष्ठित (established / स्थापित) होकर (सब कुछ) प्रतिष्ठित होगा?'
en: He (the Puruṣa) reflected (īkṣata): 'In whose departure (utkrānta) will everything depart? In whose establishment (pratiṣṭhita) will everything be established?'
gr: sa īkṣata — 'He reflected/willed': this echoes the creation-accounts of other Upanishads. The Aitareya (1.1.1): 'ātmā vā idam eka evāgra āsīt... sa aikṣata — lokān nu sṛjā iti' — 'The Self alone existed in the beginning... He saw/willed: let me create worlds.' The Chāndogya (6.2.3): 'tad aikṣata — bahu syāṁ prajāyeya' — 'It willed: may I become many, may I be born.' The double question: (1) 'In whose departure (utkrānta) will everything depart?' — the Puruṣa asked: if I leave the body, what follows me? Answer: everything — all sixteen kalās collapse when the Puruṣa departs. (2) 'In whose establishment (pratiṣṭhita) will everything be established?' — if I am present, what is established? Answer: everything — all sixteen kalās exist only because the Puruṣa sustains them. This establishes the Puruṣa as both the efficient cause (by whose will the kalās arise) and the material foundation (in whom the kalās subsist).

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'ईक्षत' — यह शब्द सिद्ध करता है कि सृष्टि का कारण चेतन (conscious) है — जड़ (inert) प्रकृति नहीं। पुरुष ने संकल्प किया — 'मेरे जाने पर सब जाएगा, मेरे रहने पर सब रहेगा' — यह पूर्ण आधिपत्य (absolute sovereignty) है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'īkṣata' — this word proves the cause of creation is conscious — not inert prakṛti. The Puruṣa willed: 'when I depart, all departs; when I remain, all remains.' This is absolute sovereignty.
advaita.ins: The universe began with a thought — 'He reflected.' Not a bang, not an accident, but a conscious act of seeing. And what He saw was: 'Everything depends on Me.' That's not arrogance — it's ontology.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'ईक्षत' — भगवान् का संकल्प (divine will) सृष्टि का मूल कारण है। 'उत्क्रान्ते उत्क्रान्तो भविष्यामि' — भगवान् जब शरीर त्यागते हैं (जीव-रूप में), तो सोलह कलाएँ भी लय (dissolve) हो जाती हैं — यह भगवान् की सर्वाधिष्ठातृता (supreme lordship) है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'īkṣata' — the Lord's will (saṅkalpa) is the root cause of creation. 'When I depart, all will depart' — when the Lord (as the jīva) leaves the body, the sixteen kalās dissolve. This is the Lord's supreme lordship.
vishisht.ins: God didn't stumble into creation. He planned it with a thought: 'In My presence, everything stands. In My absence, everything falls.' That thought is the foundation of the universe.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'ईक्षत' = चेतना का प्रथम क्रियात्मक आत्म-अवलोकन (self-reflection) — सृष्टि का बीज। 'उत्क्रान्ते/प्रतिष्ठिते' — पुरुष ही सृष्टि का आधार (foundation) और उसका प्रस्थान-बिन्दु (departure-point) दोनों है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'īkṣata' = consciousness's first operative self-reflection — the seed of creation. 'Utkrānta/pratiṣṭhita' — the Puruṣa is both the foundation and the departure-point of creation.
aurobindo.ins: Creation begins not with matter but with awareness — consciousness reflecting on itself. And it discovers: 'I am the ground. When I stand, everything stands. When I withdraw, everything dissolves.' That's not cosmology — that's the deepest fact of existence.

dp.a: The verb sa īkṣata ('He reflected' or 'He saw' or 'He willed') is one of the most philosophically important words in the Upanishads. It appears in the creation-accounts of three major Upanishads: (1) Aitareya 1.1.1: 'ātmā vā idam eka evāgra āsīt... sa aikṣata' — 'The Self alone existed in the beginning... He saw/willed.' (2) Chāndogya 6.2.3: 'tad aikṣata — bahu syāṁ prajāyeya' — 'It (Being/sat) saw: may I become many, may I be born forth.' (3) Taittirīya 2.6.1: 'so'kāmayata — bahu syāṁ prajāyeya' — 'He desired: may I become many.' Why is this verb so important? Because it establishes that the first cause of creation is conscious. The verb īkṣ (to see/reflect) can only apply to a sentient being — you cannot say that a stone 'reflected' or that unconscious matter 'saw.' This is Shankara's chief argument against the Sāṅkhya school, which posits unconscious prakṛti (nature) as the first cause. Shankara says: the Upanishads consistently use conscious verbs (īkṣata, akāmayata) for the first cause — therefore the first cause must be a conscious being (Brahman/Puruṣa), not inert matter. In the Prashna: the Puruṣa's 'reflection' establishes his absolute sovereignty — everything depends on him. His departure = universal dissolution. His establishment = universal existence.

dp.q: 🔍 The Puruṣa as both efficient and material cause
dp.a: The double question in this mantra reveals the Puruṣa's dual causality: (1) Efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa): 'In whose departure will everything depart?' — the Puruṣa's will (īkṣaṇa/saṅkalpa) initiates creation. Without his willing, nothing comes into being. He is the agent of creation. (2) Material/foundational cause (upādāna-kāraṇa): 'In whose establishment will everything be established?' — the Puruṣa is the substratum in which the sixteen kalās subsist. Without him as the foundation, the kalās have no ground of being. He is the material from which creation is constituted. The significance: in ordinary experience, the efficient cause and the material cause are different. A potter (efficient cause) shapes clay (material cause) into a pot. But in the Upanishadic account, the Puruṣa is both — like a spider that is both the weaver (efficient) and the thread (material) of its web (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.1.20). How the schools interpret this: Advaita: Brahman is both efficient and material cause; the world is a 'transformation' (vivarta) of Brahman through māyā. Vishishtadvaita: Brahman is both causes; the world is a real transformation (pariṇāma) of Brahman's body — the world is real, not illusory. Sri Aurobindo: Brahman is both causes; creation is a progressive self-manifestation of consciousness into increasingly differentiated forms.

sk: स प्राणमसृजत प्राणाच्छ्रद्धां खं वायुर्ज्योतिरापः पृथिवीन्द्रियं मनो ऽन्नमन्नाद्वीर्यं तपो मन्त्राः कर्म लोका लोकेषु च नाम च ||
ro: saḥ · prāṇam · asṛjata · prāṇāt · śraddhāṁ · khaṁ · vāyuḥ · jyotiḥ · āpaḥ · pṛthivī · indriyaṁ · manaḥ · annam · annāt · vīryaṁ · tapaḥ · mantrāḥ · karma · lokāḥ · lokeṣu · ca · nāma · ca ||
hi: उसने (पुरुष ने) प्राण को सृजा (रचा)। प्राण से — श्रद्धा, ख (आकाश), वायु, ज्योति (अग्नि/प्रकाश), आप (जल), पृथिवी, इन्द्रिय, मन, अन्न (भोजन) — (और) अन्न से — वीर्य (शक्ति), तप, मन्त्र, कर्म, लोक (worlds) — और लोकों में नाम (name / identity) — (ये सब उत्पन्न हुए)।
en: He created Prāṇa (the life-force). From Prāṇa: śraddhā (faith), kha (space/ether), vāyu (air), jyoti (light/fire), āpaḥ (water), pṛthivī (earth), indriya (the senses), manas (mind), anna (food). From anna (food): vīrya (vigour), tapas (austerity), mantrāḥ (sacred formulae), karma (action), lokāḥ (worlds) — and in the worlds, nāma (name/identity).
gr: The sixteen kalās enumerated: the Puruṣa creates Prāṇa first, then from Prāṇa a chain of sixteen emanations: (1) prāṇa, (2) śraddhā, (3) kha (space), (4) vāyu (air), (5) jyoti (fire/light), (6) āpaḥ (water), (7) pṛthivī (earth), (8) indriya (senses), (9) manas (mind), (10) anna (food), (11) vīrya (vigour), (12) tapas (austerity), (13) mantrāḥ (sacred formulae), (14) karma (ritual action), (15) lokāḥ (worlds), (16) nāma (name/identity). The order: the chain moves from the subtle to the gross (prāṇa → elements → senses → mind → food) and then from the gross back to the cultural/spiritual (food → vigour → austerity → mantra → karma → worlds → name). This is a complete cosmogony — from the Puruṣa's will to individual identity. śraddhā appears second: faith is listed before the physical elements — a surprising placement. It suggests that faith is not merely a psychological state but a cosmic principle — the 'glue' that holds creation together (cf. Chāndogya 7.19: 'śraddhā is greater than mind').

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — सोलह कलाओं की श्रृंखला (chain) दिखाती है कि सम्पूर्ण सृष्टि — पंचभूत, इन्द्रिय, मन, अन्न, कर्म, लोक, नाम — सब एक पुरुष से निकला है। जब ज्ञान (knowledge) से ये कलाएँ पुनः पुरुष में विलीन होती हैं — तब मुक्ति (liberation) है।
advaita.en: Shankara says the chain of sixteen kalās shows that all creation — elements, senses, mind, food, action, worlds, name — emerges from one Puruṣa. When through knowledge these kalās dissolve back into the Puruṣa — that is liberation.
advaita.ins: Sixteen parts — from space to name — all come from one source. The whole universe is a chain of emanations from the Puruṣa. Understand the chain, trace it back to the source, and the parts dissolve into the whole.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — सोलह कलाएँ भगवान् के शरीर (body of God) हैं। भगवान् ने प्रथम प्राण को सृजा, फिर प्राण से श्रद्धा, आकाश, वायु... इत्यादि। सम्पूर्ण सृष्टि = भगवान् का विस्तारित शरीर।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the sixteen kalās are the body of God. The Lord first created Prāṇa, then from Prāṇa: śraddhā, space, air... and so on. The entire creation = the Lord's extended body.
vishisht.ins: God's body is not a human form — it's the entire creation. The sixteen parts — from breath to name — are the limbs of His cosmic body. When you see the world, you're seeing God's body.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — सोलह कलाएँ = चेतना के क्रमिक अवरोहण (progressive descent) के सोलह चरण — सूक्ष्मतम (प्राण) से स्थूलतम (नाम) तक। यह चेतना का आत्म-प्रकटीकरण (self-manifestation) है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says the sixteen kalās = sixteen stages of consciousness's progressive descent — from the subtlest (prāṇa) to the grossest (nāma). This is consciousness's self-manifestation.
aurobindo.ins: Consciousness descends in sixteen steps — from life-force to faith to space to air to fire to water to earth to senses to mind to food to vigour to austerity to mantra to action to worlds to name. That's the ladder of creation. Climb it back up, and you find the Puruṣa.

dp.q: 🔍 The sixteen kalās — a complete cosmogony
dp.a: The Prashna Upanishad's sixteen kalās present a unique cosmogony — a complete account of how reality emanates from the Puruṣa in sixteen stages: First emanation: (1) Prāṇa (life-force) — the first creation, the bridge between consciousness and matter. From Prāṇa — the subtle-to-gross sequence: (2) Śraddhā (faith) — the cosmic 'glue'; the principle of coherence. (3) Kha (space/ether) — the first physical element, providing 'room'. (4) Vāyu (air/wind) — the principle of movement. (5) Jyoti (fire/light) — the principle of transformation. (6) Āpaḥ (water) — the principle of cohesion and fluidity. (7) Pṛthivī (earth) — the principle of solidity and support. (8) Indriya (senses) — the instruments of perception and action. (9) Manas (mind) — the coordinator of the senses. (10) Anna (food) — the material sustenance of embodied life. From Anna — the cultural-spiritual sequence: (11) Vīrya (vigour/potency) — the concentrated energy from food. (12) Tapas (austerity) — the disciplined use of energy. (13) Mantrāḥ (sacred formulae) — the verbal expressions of truth. (14) Karma (ritual action) — the purposeful deployment of energy. (15) Lokāḥ (worlds) — the cosmic spaces created by karma. (16) Nāma (name/identity) — the final individuation; each being in each world has a name. The structure: the first ten kalās cover the cosmological chain (from consciousness to physical matter). The last six cover the cultural-ritual chain (from food-energy to individual identity). Together, they span the entire range of manifest reality — from the Puruṣa's first breath to the last named individual in the last world.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is Śraddhā (faith) listed before the five elements?
dp.a: The placement of śraddhā (faith) as the second kalā — before space, air, fire, water, and earth — is one of the most striking features of this cosmogony. It elevates faith from a mere psychological attitude to a cosmic principle: What does this mean? In the Vedic worldview, creation is not a mechanical process but a purposive one. The Puruṣa wills creation (sa īkṣata). For that will to manifest, there must be a principle of coherence — something that holds the creative process together, that ensures the unfolding follows a pattern rather than dissolving into chaos. That principle is śraddhā. Śraddhā as cosmic glue: śraddhā is the 'faith' that creation has in its own process — the inherent tendency of things to hold together, to cohere, to follow their nature. Without śraddhā, prāṇa would not give rise to space, space would not give rise to air, and so on. The chain would break. Parallel texts: (1) Chāndogya 7.19: 'Śraddhā is greater than mind (manas)... When one has śraddhā, one reflects (manute); without śraddhā, one does not reflect.' Here śraddhā precedes mental activity — it is more fundamental than thought. (2) Taittirīya 1.11: 'Śraddhayā deyam' — 'Give with faith.' Śraddhā enables generosity, which enables social order, which enables civilisation. (3) Bhagavad Gītā 17.3: 'A person is made of his faith (śraddhā-mayaḥ).' You are what you have faith in. The lesson: faith is not a luxury or an add-on — it is a structural necessity of the universe. Without it, creation literally cannot cohere.

sk: स यथेमा नद्यः स्यन्दमानाः समुद्रायणाः समुद्रं प्राप्यास्तं गच्छन्ति भिद्येते तासां नामरूपे समुद्र इत्येवं प्रोच्यते एवमेवास्य परिद्रष्टुरिमाः षोडश कलाः पुरुषायणाः पुरुषं प्राप्यास्तं गच्छन्ति भिद्येते चासां नामरूपे पुरुष इत्येवं प्रोच्यते स एषो ऽकलो ऽमृतो भवति तदेष श्लोकः ||
ro: saḥ · yathā · imāḥ · nadyaḥ · syandamānāḥ · samudra-ayaṇāḥ · samudraṁ · prāpya · astaṁ · gacchanti · bhidyete · tāsāṁ · nāma-rūpe · samudraḥ · iti · eva · procyate · evam · eva · asya · paridraṣṭuḥ · imāḥ · ṣoḍaśa · kalāḥ · puruṣa-ayaṇāḥ · puruṣaṁ · prāpya · astaṁ · gacchanti · bhidyete · ca · āsāṁ · nāma-rūpe · puruṣaḥ · iti · evaṁ · procyate · saḥ · eṣaḥ · akalaḥ · amṛtaḥ · bhavati · tat · eṣaḥ · ślokaḥ ||
hi: जैसे ये नदियाँ — बहती हुई (स्यन्दमानाः) — समुद्राभिमुख (समुद्रायणाः) — समुद्र को प्राप्त होकर अस्त (विलीन) हो जाती हैं, उनके नाम-रूप (name and form) टूट जाते (भिद्येते) हैं, (और वह) 'समुद्र' ऐसे ही कहा जाता है — वैसे ही इस परिद्रष्टा (all-seeing witness) की ये सोलह कलाएँ — पुरुषाभिमुख (पुरुषायणाः) — पुरुष को प्राप्त होकर अस्त (विलीन) हो जाती हैं, उनके नाम-रूप टूट जाते हैं, (और वह) 'पुरुष' ऐसे ही कहा जाता है। वह — यह (पुरुष) — अकल (part-less / कला-रहित) और अमृत (immortal) हो जाता है। इस विषय में यह श्लोक है —
en: Just as these rivers, flowing (syandamānāḥ), ocean-bound (samudra-ayaṇāḥ), reaching the ocean, disappear (astaṁ gacchanti), and their name and form (nāma-rūpe) are broken (bhidyete) — and it is called simply 'the ocean' — so too these sixteen parts (kalāḥ) of this all-seeing witness (paridraṣṭā), bound for the Puruṣa (puruṣa-ayaṇāḥ), reaching the Puruṣa, disappear, and their name and form are broken — and he is called simply 'the Puruṣa.' He becomes part-less (akala) and immortal (amṛta). Regarding this, there is this verse —

ws.h: समुद्र की ओर जाने वाली / समुद्राभिमुख
नाम और रूप टूट जाते हैं / विलीन हो जाते हैं
सर्वद्रष्टा / सब ओर देखने वाले का

gr: The river-ocean simile: one of the most famous images in the Upanishads. Rivers (Ganges, Yamuna, etc.) flow toward the ocean. On reaching it, they lose their individual names and forms — there is no 'Ganges-water' or 'Yamuna-water' in the ocean, only 'ocean.' Similarly, the sixteen kalās (prāṇa, śraddhā, kha, etc.) flow toward the Puruṣa. When they reach him (at liberation or at the dissolution of the body), their individual identities dissolve — there is no 'prāṇa' or 'manas' or 'anna' in the Puruṣa, only 'Puruṣa.' nāma-rūpe bhidyete — 'name and form are broken': nāma-rūpa (name-and-form) is the Upanishadic term for individuation — the principle that differentiates one entity from another. When nāma-rūpa is 'broken,' differentiation ceases, and the apparent multiplicity resolves into unity. paridraṣṭā — 'the all-seeing witness': the Puruṣa is not merely a substance into which things dissolve but a witness (draṣṭā) who sees all (pari) — consciousness, not inert matter. akalaḥ amṛtaḥ bhavati — 'he becomes part-less and immortal': when the sixteen kalās dissolve, the Puruṣa stands revealed as he truly is — without parts (akala), beyond death (amṛta). The 'sixteen-part Puruṣa' was never truly sixteen-parted — the parts were superimpositions (upādhi). Remove the superimpositions, and the Puruṣa is whole.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — नदी-समुद्र उपमा अद्वैत (non-duality) का सर्वोत्तम दृष्टान्त है। जैसे नदी समुद्र में विलीन होकर नाम-रूप खो देती है — वैसे ही सोलह कलाएँ ब्रह्म में विलीन होकर नाम-रूप खो देती हैं। शेष रहता है केवल अखण्ड ब्रह्म — अकल, अमृत।
advaita.en: Shankara says the river-ocean simile is the finest illustration of non-duality (advaita). As a river dissolves into the ocean losing name and form — so the sixteen kalās dissolve into Brahman losing name and form. What remains is undivided Brahman alone — akala, amṛta.
advaita.ins: The Ganges has a name. The Yamuna has a name. But pour them into the ocean, and where is the Ganges? Where is the Yamuna? Just ocean. Similarly — space, air, fire, mind, name — pour them into the Puruṣa, and there is only the Puruṣa. Undivided. Deathless.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — नदी-उपमा दिखाती है कि सोलह कलाएँ भगवान् में लय (dissolve) होती हैं — किन्तु भगवान् स्वयं अकल (part-less) और अमृत (deathless) रहते हैं। भगवान् = समुद्र; कलाएँ = नदियाँ — भगवान् से प्रकट होती हैं, भगवान् में लौटती हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the river-simile shows the sixteen kalās dissolve into the Lord — but the Lord Himself remains akala (part-less) and amṛta (deathless). The Lord = the ocean; the kalās = the rivers — they emerge from the Lord and return to the Lord.
vishisht.ins: Rivers come from the ocean (as rain) and return to the ocean (as flow). Between the two, they have names — Ganges, Yamuna, Godavari. But the ocean never became many rivers. It was always the ocean. God is that ocean. The sixteen parts are His rivers.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — नदी-उपमा चेतना के ऊर्ध्वगमन (ascent) का चित्रण है — विभेदित चेतना (differentiated consciousness) अपने स्रोत (source) में लौटती है। 'अकल' = विभाजन-रहित चेतना। 'अमृत' = शाश्वत चेतना — काल (time) और मृत्यु (death) से परे।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says the river-simile depicts the ascent of consciousness — differentiated consciousness returning to its source. 'Akala' = undivided consciousness. 'Amṛta' = eternal consciousness — beyond time and death.
aurobindo.ins: The sixteen parts are consciousness flowing outward — diversifying into space, air, mind, name. Liberation is the reverse flow — all those streams returning to the ocean of consciousness. The ocean was never actually divided. The divisions were a play of movement.

dp.a: The river-ocean simile (nadī-samudra-upamā) is one of the most powerful and frequently cited images in the Upanishads: The image: rivers (Ganges, Yamuna, Sarasvatī, etc.) flow from their mountain sources toward the ocean. Each river has a name (nāma — 'Ganges', 'Yamuna') and a form (rūpa — its particular width, colour, speed, banks). But when a river reaches the ocean, its name and form are 'broken' (bhidyete) — they dissolve. There is no 'Ganges-portion' of the ocean. There is only ocean. The application: the sixteen kalās (prāṇa, śraddhā, space, air, fire, water, earth, senses, mind, food, vigour, tapas, mantra, karma, worlds, name) are like rivers — each has its own name and form. But they all flow toward the Puruṣa (puruṣa-ayaṇāḥ — 'Puruṣa-bound'). When they reach the Puruṣa (through knowledge, through death, through dissolution), their individual identities dissolve. What remains is simply the Puruṣa — akala (without parts) and amṛta (deathless). Three key insights: (1) The parts were never truly separate: a river's water is always H₂O — the same as the ocean's. The 'separation' was in name and form only, not in substance. Similarly, the sixteen kalās are always Brahman — their apparent separateness is a matter of naming, not of nature. (2) The dissolution is natural: rivers don't 'try' to reach the ocean — they flow there by nature. Similarly, the kalās naturally resolve into the Puruṣa. Liberation is not an achievement but a return to nature. (3) The ocean is not diminished by the rivers' arrival: the ocean doesn't grow bigger or change its nature when rivers enter it. Similarly, the Puruṣa is not altered by the dissolution of the kalās — it was always what it is.

The word akala (अकल — 'without parts', 'part-less', 'undivided') describes the Puruṣa's true nature after the sixteen kalās have dissolved: The paradox: the question was about the 'sixteen-part Puruṣa' (ṣoḍaśa-kala puruṣa). The answer reveals that the Puruṣa is actually akala — without parts. The sixteen parts are not the Puruṣa's nature but his manifestation. When the manifestation resolves, the Puruṣa stands as he truly is — whole, undivided, simple. The moon-digit analogy: the moon appears to have sixteen digits (kalās) — it waxes from new moon (no visible digits) to full moon (sixteen visible digits). But the moon itself never changes — it is always whole. The 'digits' are a function of the moon's relationship to the sun and the observer's position. Similarly, the Puruṣa's sixteen 'parts' are not real divisions in the Puruṣa but functions of his self-manifestation. Philosophical significance: 'akala' = the Puruṣa is simple (without internal complexity), indivisible (cannot be broken into components), and infinite (anything with parts is limited by its parts; the partless has no limits). This connects to the broader Vedāntic teaching that Brahman is nirguṇa (without attributes) and niravayava (without limbs/parts) — not because it lacks anything but because it is everything in an undifferentiated unity.

sk: अरा इव रथनाभौ कला यस्मिन्प्रतिष्ठिताः तं वेद्यं पुरुषं वेद यथा मा वो मृत्युः परिव्यथा इति ||
ro: arāḥ · iva · ratha-nābhau · kalāḥ · yasmin · pratiṣṭhitāḥ · taṁ · vedyaṁ · puruṣaṁ · veda · yathā · mā · vaḥ · mṛtyuḥ · parivyathā · iti ||
hi: जैसे रथ के नाभि-चक्र (hub) में अरे (spokes) प्रतिष्ठित (स्थापित) हैं — (वैसे ही) जिसमें कलाएँ प्रतिष्ठित हैं — उस वेद्य (जानने योग्य) पुरुष को जानो — जिससे मृत्यु तुम्हें व्यथित (परिव्यथा / पीड़ित) न करे।
en: As spokes (arāḥ) are fixed in the hub (nābhi) of a wheel — so are the parts (kalāḥ) established in Him. Know that Puruṣa who is to be known (vedya) — so that death may not afflict (parivyathā) you.

ws.e: in the hub of a chariot-wheel

ws.h: व्यथित करे / पीड़ित करे / दुःख दे

gr: The wheel-hub simile: arāḥ iva ratha-nābhau — 'as spokes in the hub of a wheel.' This image appears also in the Muṇḍaka (2.2.6) and the Kaṭha (2.3.1). All spokes of a wheel converge on the hub — the hub is the centre that holds all spokes together. Without the hub, the spokes collapse; without the Puruṣa, the sixteen kalās have no support. vedyaṁ puruṣam veda — 'know that Puruṣa who is to be known': the practical conclusion — know Him. Not worship, not ritual, not austerity — knowledge (vidyā) of the Puruṣa is the means to immortality. mā vaḥ mṛtyuḥ parivyathā — 'so that death may not afflict you': the purpose of knowing the Puruṣa. Death (mṛtyu) is the ultimate affliction (vyathā) of embodied existence. Knowing the part-less, deathless Puruṣa liberates one from the fear and reality of death. This is Pippalāda's blessing to his students.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — चक्र-नाभि (wheel-hub) उपमा दिखाती है कि सभी कलाएँ एक केन्द्र (पुरुष) में स्थित हैं — जैसे सभी अरे (spokes) नाभि में। 'तं वेद्यं पुरुषं वेद' — उस पुरुष को जानो — ज्ञान (knowledge) ही मृत्यु से मुक्ति का एकमात्र उपाय है।
advaita.en: Shankara says the wheel-hub simile shows all kalās are centred in one Puruṣa — as all spokes are in the hub. 'Know that Puruṣa who is to be known' — knowledge alone is the sole means of liberation from death.
advaita.ins: Sixteen spokes, one hub. Remove the hub, the wheel collapses. Know the hub — the Puruṣa — and you know the centre of everything. And when you know the centre, the circumference (death, birth, change) can't touch you.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'वेद्यं पुरुषं वेद' — भगवान् को जानना ही मृत्यु-भय से मुक्ति है। चक्र-नाभि उपमा = भगवान् सम्पूर्ण सृष्टि का केन्द्र (centre) और आधार (support) हैं — सब कुछ उनमें प्रतिष्ठित है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'vedyaṁ puruṣam veda' — knowing the Lord is liberation from the fear of death. The wheel-hub simile = the Lord is the centre and support of all creation — everything is established in Him.
vishisht.ins: All of creation revolves around God like spokes around a hub. Know the hub, and you understand why the wheel turns. Know God, and death becomes just another spoke — part of the wheel, but not the centre.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — चक्र-नाभि उपमा = चेतना का केन्द्र (centre of consciousness)। सोलह कलाएँ = चेतना की सोलह किरणें (rays) — सब केन्द्र से निकलती हैं, केन्द्र में लौटती हैं। 'मृत्युः परिव्यथा मा' = चेतन केन्द्र को जानने वाला मृत्यु से अप्रभावित (untouched) रहता है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says the wheel-hub simile = the centre of consciousness. Sixteen kalās = sixteen rays of consciousness — all emanate from the centre, all return to the centre. 'Mṛtyuḥ parivyathā mā' = one who knows the conscious centre remains untouched by death.
aurobindo.ins: You are the hub, not the spoke. The spoke moves, the hub is still. Death touches the spokes — the moving, changing parts of your existence. But the hub — the conscious centre — neither moves nor dies. Know yourself as the hub.

dp.a: The wheel-hub simile (arā-ratha-nābhi-upamā) is a recurring Upanishadic image for the relationship between the multiplicity of the world and the unity of the Self: The image: a chariot wheel has many spokes (arā) radiating from a central hub (nābhi). The hub is the centre — it holds all the spokes together, gives them structure, and enables the wheel to function. Remove the hub, and the spokes scatter; without the hub, there is no wheel. The application: the sixteen kalās are the spokes; the Puruṣa is the hub. All the parts of manifest reality (space, air, fire, water, earth, senses, mind, food, etc.) converge on the Puruṣa — he is their centre, their support, their raison d'être. Without the Puruṣa, the kalās have no coherence; they would scatter into nothing. Parallel occurrences: (1) Muṇḍaka 2.2.6: 'Where the nāḍīs (channels) are joined together like spokes in a hub — there, meditate on the Self.' (2) Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.5.15: 'As all spokes are fixed in the hub and rim of a wheel, so all beings, all gods, all worlds, all breaths, all these selves are fixed in this Self.' (3) Kaṭha 2.3.1: the eternal tree with Brahman as the root — a variation on the same idea (the root holds the tree as the hub holds the spokes). The lesson: the practical instruction is 'know that Puruṣa' — find the hub. When you know the centre, you understand the whole wheel. And you discover that the centre — unlike the spokes — does not rotate, does not wear, does not break.

dp.q: 🔍 'So that death may not afflict you' — the Upanishadic promise
dp.a: The phrase 'mā vaḥ mṛtyuḥ parivyathā' ('so that death may not afflict you') is Pippalāda's final benediction — and it encapsulates the entire purpose of Upanishadic teaching: What does 'death not afflicting' mean? It does NOT mean physical immortality — the body will die regardless of what one knows. It means: (1) Freedom from the fear of death: the knower of the Puruṣa understands that death is the dissolution of the kalās (parts), not the destruction of the Puruṣa. Since one's true nature is the Puruṣa (akala, amṛta), death cannot touch what one truly is. (2) Freedom from the cycle of death and rebirth: the knower who has realised the part-less Puruṣa is not reborn — the kalās do not reconstitute after dissolution. The river that has reached the ocean does not become a river again. (3) Freedom from the 'sting' of death: even while alive, the knower is not 'afflicted' (parivyathā = tormented, shaken) by the prospect of death — because death is understood as the natural dissolution of parts that were never ultimately real (like the 'death' of a river-name when it enters the ocean). The Upanishadic promise: this is the consistent promise across all ten principal Upanishads: know the Self, and death loses its power. The Kaṭha (1.2.18): 'The Self is not born, nor does it die.' The Īśā (11): 'By vidyā (knowledge), one crosses over death.' The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (1.3.28): 'Lead me from death to immortality.' The Prashna closes its final question with this promise — knowledge of the sixteen-part Puruṣa (who is actually part-less) is the antidote to death.

ro: tān · ha · uvāca · etāvat · eva · aham · etat · paraṁ · brahma · veda · na · ataḥ · param · asti · iti ||
hi: उनसे (शिष्यों से) उन्होंने (पिप्पलाद ने) कहा — 'मैं इतना ही (एतावत् एव) इस पर ब्रह्म (Supreme Brahman) को जानता हूँ। इससे परे (अतः परम्) कुछ नहीं है (नास्ति)।'
en: To them he said: 'This much alone (etāvat eva) I know of this Supreme Brahman (para brahma). There is nothing higher (param) than this (ataḥ).'

ws.e: there is nothing higher than this

gr: The teacher's conclusion: Pippalāda declares that his teaching is complete — 'etāvat eva' ('this much only') — and that there is nothing beyond para Brahman. This is both a statement of completeness (the six questions have covered the entire range of Brahman-knowledge) and of humility (the teacher acknowledges the limits of verbal teaching — Brahman transcends all words). na ataḥ param asti — 'there is nothing higher': this echoes the Bhagavad Gītā (7.7): 'mattaḥ parataraṁ nānyat kiñcid asti dhanañjaya' — 'There is nothing higher than Me, O Arjuna.' It is the final assertion — the Puruṣa is the ultimate reality, the ground of all grounds, beyond which inquiry cannot go.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'नातः परमस्ति' — पर ब्रह्म सर्वोच्च है — इससे ऊपर कुछ नहीं। 'एतावदेव' — शिक्षण (teaching) की सीमा यहीं है; जो शेष है वह अनुभव (direct experience) का विषय है, शब्दों (words) का नहीं।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'na ataḥ param asti' — the Supreme Brahman is the highest — nothing is above it. 'Etāvat eva' — the limit of teaching is here; what remains is the subject of direct experience (anubhava), not words.
advaita.ins: Pippalāda has said everything that can be said. The rest is silence — not because he's holding back, but because Brahman is beyond words. He's taken you to the edge of language. The next step is yours.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'नातः परमस्ति' — भगवान् (परब्रह्म) से ऊपर कोई तत्त्व नहीं। पिप्पलाद ने छह प्रश्नों में भगवान् के सम्पूर्ण स्वरूप (प्राण, सृष्टि, चेतना, ओंकार, कलाएँ) का वर्णन किया — अब शिष्यों को भगवद्-अनुभव (God-experience) की ओर जाना है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'na ataḥ param asti' — nothing is higher than the Lord (para Brahman). Pippalāda has described the Lord's complete nature through six questions (prāṇa, creation, consciousness, OM, kalās). Now the disciples must proceed to God-experience.
vishisht.ins: Six questions, six answers — and the teacher says: 'That's all there is. There is nothing higher than God.' Not 'I've run out of things to say' but 'I've shown you the highest thing. Now go and experience it.'

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'एतावत् एव' — बौद्धिक ज्ञान (intellectual knowledge) की सीमा। 'नातः परम्' — चेतना का चरम लक्ष्य (ultimate goal) प्राप्त हो गया — अब अनुभूति (realisation) शेष है, जो शब्दातीत (beyond words) है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'etāvat eva' — the limit of intellectual knowledge. 'Na ataḥ param' — the ultimate goal of consciousness has been indicated. What remains is realisation (anubhūti), which is beyond words.
aurobindo.ins: Words have done their job. The teacher has pointed. The finger (teaching) is not the moon (Brahman). Now put down the finger and look at the moon directly.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'nothing higher than this' mean?
dp.a: Pippalāda's declaration 'na ataḥ param asti' ('there is nothing higher than this') is one of the strongest assertions in the Upanishads. It means: (1) Ontological finality: para Brahman is the ultimate reality — the ground of all grounds. There is no 'super-Brahman' beyond Brahman, no further layer to uncover. The search for the ultimate ends here. This is echoed in the Bhagavad Gītā (7.7): 'mattaḥ parataraṁ nānyat kiñcid asti' — 'There is nothing whatsoever higher than Me.' (2) Epistemic completeness: Pippalāda has taught everything that can be taught about Brahman. The six questions have covered: (Q1) cosmology — who creates?; (Q2) physiology — who sustains?; (Q3) origin of prāṇa — whence life?; (Q4) consciousness — who sleeps, dreams, wakes?; (Q5) practice — how to reach Brahman?; (Q6) metaphysics — what is the structure of reality? Together, these six questions span the entire field of Brahman-inquiry. (3) Pedagogical closure: the teacher signals that the teaching is complete. There is no seventh question, no further lesson. What remains is not more information but direct realisation (sākṣātkāra) — and that cannot be transmitted by words. (4) Apophatic humility: 'etāvat eva' ('this much only') can also be read as: 'words can go only this far.' The teacher has brought the students to the edge of language. Brahman itself is beyond language — 'yato vāco nivartante' (Taittirīya 2.9) — 'from which words return, unable to reach.'

dp.q: 🔍 Structure of the Prashna Upanishad — six questions as a complete system
dp.a: The six questions of the Prashna Upanishad form a complete philosophical system: Question 1 (Kabandhin): Cosmology — 'Who sustains the world?' Answer: Prāṇa (life-force) and Rayi (matter), manifesting as Sun (time-giver) and Moon (food-giver). The two cosmic paths: devayāna (path of the gods, sun, no return) and pitṛyāna (path of the ancestors, moon, return). Question 2 (Bhārgava): Physiology — 'How many gods support a creature?' Answer: five elements + speech + mind + eye + ear — but Prāṇa is supreme among them (bee-queen simile). Question 3 (Kausalya): Origin of life — 'Whence is Prāṇa born?' Answer: from the Ātman (shadow-simile). Fivefold division (prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, vyāna). 101 nāḍīs. Macrocosm-microcosm correspondence. Question 4 (Gārgya): Consciousness — 'What sleeps and what is awake?' Answer: three states of consciousness (waking, dream, deep sleep). Sun-ray simile for sleep. Mind as dreamer. Ātman's light in deep sleep. Bird-tree simile. All rests in the akṣara ātman. Question 5 (Satyakāma): Practice — 'What is the fruit of OM-meditation?' Answer: three levels (one mātrā → earth; two mātrās → moon; three mātrās → Brahman). Integration principle. Five attributes of Brahman: śānta, ajara, amṛta, abhaya, para. Question 6 (Sukeśā): Metaphysics — 'Where is the sixteen-part Person?' Answer: within the body. Sixteen kalās enumerated. River-ocean simile: the kalās dissolve into the Puruṣa, who is akala (part-less) and amṛta (immortal). Wheel-hub simile: know the Puruṣa, and death cannot afflict you. The progression: Cosmology → Physiology → Life-origin → Consciousness → Practice → Ultimate Reality. From the outermost (the cosmos) to the innermost (the Puruṣa within). A complete journey from 'what is the world?' to 'who am I?'

sk: ते तमर्चयन्तस्त्वं हि नः पिता यो ऽस्माकमविद्यायाः परं पारं तारयसीति नमः परमऋषिभ्यो नमः परमऋषिभ्यः ||
ro: te · tam · arcayantaḥ · tvaṁ · hi · naḥ · pitā · yaḥ · asmākam · avidyāyāḥ · paraṁ · pāraṁ · tārayasi · iti · namaḥ · parama-ṛṣibhyaḥ · namaḥ · parama-ṛṣibhyaḥ ||
hi: वे (छहों शिष्य) उन्हें (पिप्पलाद को) पूजते हुए (अर्चयन्तः) (बोले) — 'आप ही हमारे पिता (pitā) हैं — जो हमें अविद्या (ignorance) से परम पार (the farthest shore) तक पहुँचाते हैं (तारयसि)।' परम ऋषियों को नमस्कार! परम ऋषियों को नमस्कार!
en: They, honouring (arcayantaḥ) him, (said): 'You indeed are our father (pitā) — you who ferry us across (tārayasi) to the far shore (para pāra) beyond ignorance (avidyā).' Salutation to the supreme seers (parama-ṛṣibhyaḥ)! Salutation to the supreme seers!

ws.h: पूजा करते हुए / सम्मान करते हुए
परम पार / दूसरा किनारा / अन्तिम तट
पार कराते हो / तैराकर ले जाते हो
श्रेष्ठ ऋषियों को / परम ऋषियों को

gr: The closing tribute: the six disciples honour Pippalāda with the highest title — pitā (father). In the Vedic tradition, the guru is considered a second father because he gives the student a second birth — the birth into knowledge. The biological father gives the body; the guru gives understanding. avidyāyāḥ paraṁ pāraṁ tārayasi — 'you ferry us across to the far shore beyond ignorance': the ocean-crossing metaphor. Avidyā (ignorance) is an ocean; the teacher is the boatman; knowledge is the boat; the far shore (para pāra) is Brahman/liberation. The verb tārayasi (causative of √tṝ) means 'you make us cross' — the teacher actively carries the student across. namaḥ parama-ṛṣibhyaḥ — 'salutation to the supreme seers': repeated twice, closing the Upanishad with a double salutation to the lineage of teachers (guru-paramparā) who transmitted this knowledge from generation to generation. The repetition expresses overflowing devotion.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'अविद्यायाः परं पारं तारयसि' — गुरु अविद्या-सागर (ocean of ignorance) से पार कराते हैं — यही गुरु का सर्वोच्च कार्य है। 'परमऋषिभ्यो नमः' — गुरु-परम्परा (teacher-lineage) को प्रणाम — ज्ञान की अखण्ड श्रृंखला (unbroken chain) जो ब्रह्मा से आज तक चली आ रही है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'avidyāyāḥ paraṁ pāraṁ tārayasi' — the guru ferries across the ocean of ignorance — this is the guru's supreme function. 'Namaḥ parama-ṛṣibhyaḥ' — salutation to the guru-paramparā — the unbroken chain of knowledge from Brahmā to the present.
advaita.ins: The Upanishad ends not with a grand philosophical statement but with a bow. Six students touch their teacher's feet and say: 'You are our father. You carried us across the ocean of ignorance.' That's the deepest teaching: knowledge is received, not taken. Grace makes it possible.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'त्वं हि नः पिता' — आचार्य (guru) भगवान् का प्रतिनिधि (representative) है — भगवान् की कृपा (grace) गुरु के माध्यम से बहती है। 'परमऋषिभ्यो नमः' — भगवान् से प्रारम्भ होने वाली गुरु-श्रृंखला (teacher-chain) को नमन।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'tvaṁ hi naḥ pitā' — the teacher (ācārya) is the Lord's representative — the Lord's grace flows through the teacher. 'Namaḥ parama-ṛṣibhyaḥ' — salutation to the teacher-chain originating from the Lord.
vishisht.ins: The guru is not God — but God teaches through the guru. When the student bows to the teacher, he bows to the entire chain of teachers stretching back to God Himself. That chain is unbroken. That chain is alive. You are its newest link.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'अविद्यायाः पारं तारयसि' — गुरु अज्ञान (unconsciousness) के सागर से चेतन तट (the shore of consciousness) तक ले जाते हैं। उपनिषद् का अन्तिम शब्द कृतज्ञता (gratitude) है — ज्ञान प्राप्त करने की सबसे गहरी पूर्व-शर्त।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'avidyāyāḥ pāraṁ tārayasi' — the guru carries from the ocean of unconsciousness to the shore of consciousness. The Upanishad's last word is gratitude — the deepest prerequisite for receiving knowledge.
aurobindo.ins: The Prashna Upanishad's last word is not a doctrine — it's a thank-you. Six seekers bow and say: 'Father, you carried us across.' That gratitude is itself the far shore. The moment you are grateful for the teaching, you have understood it.

dp.a: The disciples call Pippalāda 'pitā' (father) — the highest honour a student can give a teacher in the Vedic tradition: Two births, two fathers: in the Vedic framework, a person has two births: (1) the physical birth from the mother's womb — presided over by the biological father; (2) the spiritual birth (upanayana / initiation) — presided over by the guru. The Manu Smṛti (2.146) says: 'The teacher who gives the Veda-birth (brahma-janma) is more venerable than the father who gave the body-birth (śarīra-janma).' Why 'father' and not 'teacher'? Because the guru does more than inform — he transforms. Information can come from books; transformation requires a living presence. The guru's role is to carry (tārayasi) the student across the ocean of ignorance — an active, personal, caring role, like a father carrying a child across a river. The guru-paramparā: the double salutation 'namaḥ parama-ṛṣibhyaḥ, namaḥ parama-ṛṣibhyaḥ' honours not just Pippalāda but the entire lineage of teachers through whom this knowledge has been transmitted — from the original seer (ṛṣi) who 'saw' the truth, through generation after generation of teachers, to the present moment. The knowledge is alive because the chain is unbroken.

The Prashna Upanishad (प्रश्नोपनिषद्) belongs to the Atharvaveda and is structured as six questions posed by six seekers to the sage Pippalāda: Setting: six seekers — Kabandhin, Bhārgava, Kausalya, Gārgya, Satyakāma, and Sukeśā — approach Pippalāda seeking Brahman-knowledge. He asks them to stay for one year of tapas, brahmacharya, and śraddhā, and then ask their questions. Q1 — Cosmology: Prāṇa (life) and Rayi (matter) create and sustain the world. Two paths after death: devayāna (sun, no return) and pitṛyāna (moon, return). Q2 — Physiology: among the bodily devas (senses + elements), Prāṇa is supreme — the bee-queen without whom all collapse. Q3 — Origin of Prāṇa: Prāṇa arises from the Ātman (shadow-simile), divides fivefold, travels through 101 nāḍīs, and mirrors the macrocosm. Q4 — Consciousness: three states (waking, dream, deep sleep). Sun-ray simile for sleep. Mind's creative power in dreams. Ātman's light in deep sleep. All rests in the imperishable Self. Q5 — Practice: OM-meditation at three depths (one/two/three mātrās) reaches three destinations (earth/moon/Brahman). Full OM = liberation. Q6 — Metaphysics: the sixteen-part Puruṣa is within the body. The sixteen kalās dissolve into the Puruṣa like rivers into the ocean. The Puruṣa is akala (part-less) and amṛta (immortal). Know Him, and death cannot afflict you. Conclusion: Pippalāda declares: 'There is nothing higher than this.' The students honour him as father and bow to the lineage of supreme seers.
